section.title: Warning Against Antichrists
section.sectionRationale: John turns from the world's pull to the sharpest danger inside the church: antichrists who deny that Jesus is the Christ. He explains that they went out from the fellowship because they never truly belonged, names the lie as denial of the Son, and reassures believers that the anointing they have keeps them in the truth.
section.thesis: In the last hour many antichrists deny that Jesus is the Christ and so deny the Father and the Son, but believers, taught and secured by the anointing they have received, must let the truth they heard from the beginning remain in them and so remain in the Son and the Father, who has promised them eternal life.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the last hour and the many antichrists; the lie that denies the Son and the Father; the call to let the truth remain and so remain in Christ; and the anointing that teaches and secures believers.

units.label: The last hour and the antichrists
units.note: those who went out from us

verses.text: Children, it is the last hour; and just as you have heard that the {{antichristos|antichrist}} is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour.
They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But their departure made it clear that none of them belonged to us.

units.label: The lie that denies the Son

verses.text: You, however, have an {{chrisma|anointing}} from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.
I have not written to you because you lack knowledge of the truth, but because you have it, and because no lie comes from the truth.
Who is the liar, if it is not the one who {{arneomai|denies}} that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son.
Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.

units.label: Let the truth remain in you

verses.text: As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning {{meno|remain}} in you. If it does, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father.
And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life.
I have written these things to you about those who are trying to {{planao|deceive}} you.

And as for you, the anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him as you have been taught.

antichristos.gloss: Antichrist, one who stands against and in place of Christ. John uses it both for a coming figure his readers had heard about and for the many present deniers of Jesus already at work. To reject that Jesus is the Christ, the Son, is to embody the very spirit of antichrist.

chrisma.gloss: Anointing, that which is smeared or applied, here the anointing believers have received from the Holy One. It is closely tied to the Holy Spirit and the truth taught by Him. The word plays on Christ, the Anointed One: those who belong to the Anointed share His anointing and so know the truth.

arneomai.gloss: To deny, disown, refuse, renounce. The liar denies that Jesus is the Christ, disowning the Son. This is not honest doubt but a settled repudiation of the truth about Jesus, and John says it severs a person from the Father as well as the Son.

meno.gloss: To remain, abide, continue, dwell. John's key word for lasting fellowship. If the truth heard from the beginning remains in the believer, the believer remains in the Son and the Father. Abiding in the message and abiding in God are bound together; to hold the truth is to hold Him.

planao.gloss: To lead astray, deceive, cause to wander. The false teachers are actively trying to make believers wander from the truth about Christ. The word pictures being led off the path; John writes to keep his readers from being pulled away by these deceivers.

basic.context: John warns that it is the last hour, the stretch of time between Christ's first and second comings, and a sign of it is the appearing of many antichrists. These were teachers who had been part of the church but left, showing they never truly belonged. Their lie is denying that Jesus is the Christ, and John says that whoever denies the Son loses the Father too. But he reassures believers: they have an anointing from God that keeps them in the truth, so they must let what they first heard remain in them.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage teaches both discernment and assurance. It defines the antichrist not mainly as a future world ruler but as anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ, the Son. And it comforts believers that they are not defenceless: the Spirit's anointing teaches and secures them. Verse 27, that you do not need anyone to teach you, is not against all teaching but against the deceivers, since John himself is teaching them.
basic.originalLanguages: It is the last hour, and many an antichristos, antichrist, has appeared. Believers have a chrisma, an anointing, from the Holy One, so they know the truth. The liar is the one who denies, arneomai, that Jesus is the Christ. John urges them to let the truth remain, meno, in them and so remain in God, and he writes because deceivers are trying to lead them astray, planao.
basic.typology: The coming of antichrists in the last hour fulfils the pattern of false prophets who arose among God's people, now intensified as the age of the Messiah dawns. The anointing believers receive answers the anointing of priests, kings, and prophets, now given to all God's people by the Spirit.
basic.christ: The whole test centres on Jesus: to confess that He is the Christ, the Son, is to have the Father; to deny Him is to lose the Father. Christ is the content of the faith once heard, the one in whom believers remain, and the giver of the promise, eternal life.
basic.god: God the Father cannot be had apart from the Son; to deny the Son is to deny the Father. God secures His people by His Spirit's anointing and by the truth He first gave them, and He has bound Himself by promise to give them eternal life.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 24 warns of false christs and false prophets in the last days. John 16:13 promises the Spirit who guides into all truth. John 14:6 and John 17:3 tie knowing the Father to the Son and to eternal life.
basic.oneStory: As the age of Messiah dawns, the conflict between truth and lie sharpens, and deceivers deny the very Christ the story has been building toward. Yet God keeps His people by His Spirit and His word, so that those who hold to the Son hold the Father, and receive the eternal life promised through the whole of Scripture.

context.literary:
This section is built as a tight argument in three movements, with the claim of verse 24 as its pivot. Verses 18 and 19 give the diagnosis, a church that has been wounded by a departure. Verses 20 to 23 move to the doctrinal centre, where the issue is stated as a question about who the liar is. Verses 24 to 27 then give the remedy, which is to keep hold of what was heard at the start. John uses the same word, 'remain,' on both sides of the story. Those who left did not remain, verse 19, and those who stay are told to let the message remain in them, verse 24, and then reminded that the anointing remains in them, verse 27.

The section is also stitched together by the Greek phrase 'from the beginning,' which John has used already in 1:1 and 2:7, 'what was from the beginning.' The antichrists bring a new teaching, and John's answer is that the old one is the true one. The word 'you' appears with unusual emphasis at the start of verse 20 and again in verses 24 and 27, so that the readers are repeatedly set apart from 'they' of verse 19. Behind the rhetoric is a deliberate contrast between 'they' and 'you,' the ones who left and the ones who stayed, and the whole passage tells the second group why they should stay.

A second small structure sits inside verses 22 and 23. John asks a question and answers it in a chain, each clause building on the last: the liar, the antichrist, the one who denies the Son, the one who therefore lacks the Father, and, in the mirror image, the one who confesses the Son and so has the Father. That is a compact piece of parallelism, and it gives the doctrine in two halves, a negative statement followed by its positive twin. The passage sits within the letter's long alternation of moral and doctrinal tests, and it is where the doctrinal test comes to the front.
context.historical:
The picture behind these verses is a congregation, or a group of congregations, that had been split. Some members, who are described as having gone 'out from us,' left the fellowship and began teaching something different about Jesus. John does not name them or their system, and a careful reader should resist filling in what the text leaves blank. Still, the letter gives clues. The denial in verse 22 is about whether Jesus is the Christ, and 4:2 and 2 John 7 say that the opponents would not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Early church writers, such as Irenaeus in the late second century, reported that John wrote against a teacher named Cerinthus, who separated the heavenly Christ from the man Jesus. That is a later tradition and cannot be proved from the letter, but it fits the kind of denial John describes.

The phrase 'the last hour' would have sounded familiar to those who knew Jesus' warnings that false christs and false prophets would arise before the end, Matthew 24:4-5 and 24. Paul had spoken to the Thessalonians about the rebellion and the man of lawlessness, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-8, and Paul told the Ephesian elders that men would rise from their own number to draw away disciples, Acts 20:29-30. John's readers had been taught this expectation, since he says they heard that the antichrist is coming. His contribution is to tell them that the pattern was already visible.

There is a pastoral setting as well. A church that watches trusted people walk away is shaken, and tempted to ask whether the faith was ever real. John writes to answer that grief and to keep the remnant steady. He also writes to people who are bombarded by confident teachers, in a world where wandering preachers and new philosophies competed in every city. The community's reply was neither to become suspicious of everyone nor to follow whoever sounded wise, but to hold what had been given from the beginning.
context.canonical:
The idea of an opponent who rises against God's people and God's anointed runs through Scripture long before John gives it a name. Daniel sees a king who 'will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints,' Daniel 7:25, and a king who exalts himself above every god, Daniel 11:36. Jesus warns of false christs and false prophets who perform signs to deceive even the elect, Matthew 24:24. Paul gives the figure the title 'man of lawlessness,' 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, and Revelation 13 draws the beast who makes war on the saints. John's word 'antichrist' appears nowhere in those texts, only in his own letters, and he uses it in a broader way than any of them. In 1 John 2:18 there is both the coming one and the many already here, and in 4:3 and 2 John 7 it is a spirit and a deceiver that can be found in his own day.

The word 'anointing' links the passage to a different strand. Priests were anointed, Exodus 29:7, kings were anointed, 1 Samuel 16:13, and prophets were anointed, 1 Kings 19:16. Isaiah 61:1 speaks of one on whom the Spirit rests because the LORD has anointed him, and Jesus reads it as His own in Luke 4:18. Peter says God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and with power, Acts 10:38. Joel 2:28 promises that the Spirit will be poured out on all people, and Jeremiah 31:34 promises that all will know the LORD, which is the background to John's statement that believers 'know the truth' and need no one else to teach them.

The remaining theme is endurance. John 8:31 says that those who continue in Jesus' word are truly His disciples, and John 15:4 to 6 sets the picture of the vine and branches beside the 'remain' of verses 24 and 27. Hebrews 3:14 says believers come to share in Christ if they hold firmly to the end. These passages make verse 19 a New Testament doctrine and not an isolated comment.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John's first aim is pastoral. He writes after a painful division, and he does not want the people who remain to conclude that they were wrong to trust the apostolic message, or that the departure of teachers with more apparent wisdom means the gospel is in doubt. He tells them what the departure proves: that the visible church includes people who were never joined to it in heart, and that the church is not weakened when such people leave. He states it as a fact about the community and not as a rule for treating the people involved.

His second aim is to give a clear and short test. In a time of many voices, a believer who cannot judge every doctrinal fine point can still ask what a teaching says about Jesus. Does it confess Him as the Christ and the Son of the Father, or does it empty that confession of its content? John is not inviting suspicion toward everyone who disagrees with him over lesser matters, and the repeated link between Son and Father shows that the test is about the person and work of Christ.

His third aim is to give assurance by pointing to what God has already done. The readers have the anointing, they know the truth, and they have the promise of eternal life. The letter does not ask them to produce certainty from within but to remain where they began. The whole passage is meant to be heard by people who are afraid, and it speaks to them as a father speaks to children who have seen something frightening.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a situation and prescribes a response. The situation is that some had left the fellowship, and John explains what that meant. That is a description, and it should not be turned into a general rule that anyone who leaves a church is for that reason an antichrist, or was never saved. John speaks of those who denied that Jesus is the Christ, and the test he applies is about teaching on the Son.

What John prescribes is clear and can be taken straight across. Believers are to hold to what they have heard from the beginning, to confess the Son, and to stay in Him. They are to be wary of those who try to lead them astray. John's remark that they have no need of anyone to teach them is a statement about the anointing that the believers received, and it comes with the instruction to remain as they have been taught. It does not remove the place of teachers, pastors or the apostolic writings, since John himself is teaching in the same breath. It is a reminder that the believer's confidence rests on the Spirit's own work and not on the opinions of the latest voice.

debates.question: Who is 'the antichrist,' and how does he relate to the 'many antichrists'?

views.label: A future individual
views.case: Some readers hold that John has in mind the figure the church had been taught to expect, the man of lawlessness of 2 Thessalonians 2 or the beast of Revelation 13, and that the many antichrists are forerunners. They note that John says 'the antichrist is coming' and that the readers 'have heard' this, which suggests a known expectation.

views.label: A principle or spirit embodied in many
views.case: Others point out that John never speaks of a single person in his letters. In 4:3 it is a spirit that is already in the world, and in 2 John 7 any person who refuses to confess Christ's coming in the flesh is 'the deceiver and the antichrist.' On this reading the 'antichrist' is a type that is realised wherever the denial appears.

views.label: Both, already and not yet
views.case: Many take the passage as holding the two together: the expected opponent has not yet reached his full form, but his spirit is at work now. This matches Paul's remark that the mystery of lawlessness is 'already at work,' 2 Thessalonians 2:7.

debates.bearing: John's practical point does not depend on which view is right. Whatever the final shape of the enemy, the test for the readers is their present confession about Jesus, and they are to be watchful now.

debates.question: What does 'they went out from us, but they did not belong to us' say about those who fall away?

views.label: They were never truly saved
views.case: The reading that has been common since Augustine and the Reformers takes verse 19 at face value: had they belonged, they would have remained. Perseverance is the mark of real faith, and a departure reveals what was always the case, as Jesus indicates in John 8:31 and 15:6.

views.label: They belonged and fell away
views.case: Others, pointing to Hebrews 6:4-6 and to warnings such as John 15:6, argue that the verse addresses these particular opponents and does not rule out that a true believer could abandon the faith. They note that John says 'they did not belong' of these teachers, not of every departing person.

views.label: The verse is about visible membership
views.case: A third view stresses that John is talking about the outward fellowship and the manifest sign of inner reality, and that he does not claim to know the hearts of all who leave. He tells the readers what their departure exposes in these specific cases.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that John's words are meant to steady the remaining believers and not to give permission to judge individuals. What John clearly teaches is that endurance in the apostolic message is the evidence that one belongs to Christ, and that the church's loss of such people does not damage the gospel.

study.originalLanguages:
John's compound word antichristos is built from christos, 'anointed,' with the prefix anti, which can mean 'against' and can mean 'in place of.' Both senses fit the passage, since the opponents oppose Christ and also offer a substitute for Him. The word is found in the New Testament only in John's letters: here, in 2:22, in 4:3 and in 2 John 7. It is not used by Paul or in Revelation, and John does not use it of a single political ruler.

The next word to notice is chrisma, 'anointing,' in verses 20 and 27. It shares its root with christos and with the verb for anointing, so that those who confess the Christ have received a chrisma from Him, a share in His own title. In the New Testament it occurs only in these two verses in this letter. The word can describe the oil itself or the thing given. John does not say whether it is the Spirit directly, or the word the Spirit applies, and verse 24 hints at the second since what the believers 'heard' is to remain in them. There is also a textual detail: in verse 20 some manuscripts read 'you know all things' where the BSB reads 'all of you know the truth.' Either way, the stress falls on the whole community having what the opponents claimed to give to a select few.

The verb of verse 19, 'they went out,' is exelthan, and the preposition ek, 'out of,' is repeated in a play on words: 'they went out ek us, but they were not ek us.' The Greek construction of verse 19 is also finely balanced. The wording after 'that it might be made plain' is 'that not all are of us,' which can mean 'not all' or, as the BSB takes it, 'none.' The statement 'if they had belonged to us, they would have remained' is a contrary-to-fact condition, a way of saying that the outcome shows what was true all along.

In verse 22 the verb arneomai, 'deny,' is a present participle, 'the one who is denying,' which describes a continuing stance. Jesus uses the same verb when He says that whoever denies Him before men He will deny before the Father, Matthew 10:33. Its opposite in verse 23, 'confess,' is homologeo, 'to say the same thing,' to speak in agreement with what God has said. John uses it again for the test of the spirits in 4:2.

The last word is planao, 'to deceive,' in verse 26. Its root idea is wandering, going astray, so the deceivers are 'trying to make you wander.' Jesus uses the same verb for the many who will come in His name and 'deceive many,' Matthew 24:4-5. The present tense suggests that this is going on now.

typology.type: The anointing of priests, kings and prophets
typology.fulfillment: In Israel the anointed were set apart for service and given authority, Exodus 29:7, 1 Samuel 16:13, 1 Kings 19:16. These offices come together in Jesus, whose very title Christ means Anointed One, and who read Isaiah 61:1 as His own, Luke 4:18. In John's verse the title and the gift pass to His people: they have a chrisma from the Holy One. The escalation is from a few specially chosen individuals to every believer, as Joel 2:28 had promised. The type falls short because Israel's anointing was outward oil on selected persons, while this one is the inner teaching of the Spirit given to all.

typology.type: The false prophet who leads Israel astray
typology.fulfillment: Deuteronomy 13:1-3 provides a pattern for a prophet who works signs and still invites the people to follow other gods; Israel was to refuse him because the LORD was testing whether they loved Him. In John the opponents are different, since they are teachers of a distorted Christ and not a foreign god, but the shape is the same: a voice arises from within the community, speaks with apparent authority, and tests the people's loyalty. It is fulfilled in the antichrists of the last hour, and the test is intensified because the standard is now the Son, as John says, 'whoever denies the Son does not have the Father.' The type is imperfect because the prophets of Deuteronomy led people to idols, while John's opponents claim the name of Christ.

typology.type: Those who went out, as Judas went out
typology.fulfillment: The Gospel of John records that when Judas received the morsel he went out into the night, John 13:30, and that many disciples turned back after the hard teaching of John 6:66, leaving the Twelve with Peter's confession that Jesus is the Holy One of God, John 6:69. Those scenes foreshadow 1 John 2:19. The same verb of going out is used, and the same lesson holds, that departure from Jesus sometimes unmasks what was never right. The escalation is that what was an event in Jesus' own circle becomes a recurring mark of the whole age. The type falls short in that John 6 and 13 describe specific people and John 2 speaks of a pattern.

typology.type: The exalted king who opposes the saints
typology.fulfillment: Daniel's vision of a king who exalts himself above every god and speaks against the Most High, Daniel 7:25 and 11:36, gives the Old Testament shape that later writers apply to the enemy of the last days. Paul's man of lawlessness, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, and John's beast, Revelation 13:1-8, carry the figure further. John in his letter pulls the pattern toward the denial of the Son. The correspondence is that each version attacks the worship that belongs to God alone and challenges His people. The type is not exact, since John never ties the term antichrist to these texts, and the connection should be held with some care.

study.christ:
The whole passage is a short argument about Christ, and it never leaves Him. The question in verse 22 is who the liar is, and the answer is 'the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ.' That is not a test of manners or of loyalty to a church party. It is a question about who Jesus is, and John gives it the greatest weight possible: to deny the Son is to lose the Father, and to confess the Son is to have the Father as well. The link is not a minor consequence. It is the teaching of Jesus Himself, who said, 'No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6, and who prayed that eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent, John 17:3.

Christ also gives the passage its vocabulary. The word 'antichrist' makes sense only against the title Christ, the Anointed One. The Gospels present Jesus as the one on whom the Spirit rests, Luke 4:18, and as the one God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power, Acts 10:38. That is the title John uses and the title his opponents were emptying of meaning. Whoever says that the Christ of God and the man Jesus are two different persons, or that Jesus is not the Christ, takes away the very thing the Old Testament had promised. In the letter's wider argument, 4:2 and 2 John 7, the denial is specifically of the Christ who has come in the flesh, which means that His real humanity is as precious as His divine sonship.

He is also the source of the anointing. The Holy One of verse 20 is most naturally Jesus Himself, since 'Holy One of God' is a title used of Him in Mark 1:24 and John 6:69. The anointing flows from Him, as He said it would: He promised the Spirit of truth to His disciples, John 14:16-17, who would teach them all things and remind them of all He had said, John 14:26. When John tells his readers they have been taught, he is pointing to the continuing work of Christ through the Spirit.

Finally, Christ is the one in whom the believers remain and the one who makes the promise. 'This is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life.' That promise is fulfilled in His own life, death and resurrection, and it is held out to those who stay with Him. The picture of the vine in John 15:4 to 6 is the Lord's own commentary on 'remain.'

A caution is in order. John does not tell us that the antichrists of his day were a literal fulfilment of any particular prophecy, and readers should resist reading Christ into every detail. What the passage does teach is that every attempt to reduce Jesus, however learned, turns the church from the Father, and that the true Christ is known by those who keep what the apostles passed on.
study.god:
The Father and the Son are bound together here more closely than anywhere else in the letter. Verse 23 says that whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, and whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well. That is a statement about how God is known: He is not known in general terms apart from the One He sent. A person cannot honour God while setting aside the Son, because the Father has bound His own identity to the Son. This is a doctrine of God as much as of Christ. It speaks of a unity that includes distinction, since the Father is the Father of the Son, and the passage keeps them together in the same breath, as Jesus did in John 17:3.

The passage also shows God as one who protects His people from within. He has given an anointing that stays with them, and verse 27 speaks of that anointing as teaching them about all things and as 'true and genuine,' the opposite of the deceivers. The Spirit is the means, and the language reflects Jesus' promise of the Advocate who would guide them into all truth, John 16:13. The God of this passage does not leave His children in the hands of whichever teacher is most persuasive. He is present in them, and what He teaches is consistent with what was heard from the beginning.

God is also a faithful promiser. Verse 25 calls eternal life a promise 'that He Himself made to us.' That wording gives weight to everything else. The reader is asked to remain, but the footing is that God has said what He will give, and He does not change His mind. The tests of the letter are not designed to make believers anxious about whether God will keep His word. They are designed to tell the difference between those who have the promise and those who have walked away from it.

The passage also quietly shows the sovereignty of God over what looks like loss. A group leaves, and John says the departure 'made it clear' who belonged. God's purposes are not defeated by division; even a painful loss serves to reveal what is true. That does not make the loss painless, and John writes with evident concern, but it does mean the church can rest in a God who is not caught off guard.

For worship, the passage invites a confidence that is neither proud nor anxious. We confess the Son because the Father has made Him known, and we stay because the Spirit has taught us. The right response to a church that has been shaken is not to hunt for villains but to return to what was given, and to rest in the God who keeps what He promises.

crossReferences.note: Jesus warns that many will come in His name saying 'I am the Christ' and will deceive many. John's 'many antichrists' in verse 18 recall this warning, and his verb for deceiving is the same word Jesus uses.

Paul speaks of the rebellion, the man of lawlessness and the mystery of lawlessness already at work. It gives the future side of the picture that John knew his readers had heard, and it shows that the pattern was already operating in the first century.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders that men would rise from among them to draw disciples away. It is the closest parallel to 1 John 2:19, the opponents coming out of the church itself, and it comes from the same city tradition.

The letter returns to the test and gives it a clearer form: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. It also says that the spirit of the antichrist is already in the world, which confirms that John's use of the word is wider than a single figure.

The second letter names the deceivers who refuse to confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh and says whoever remains in the teaching of Christ has both the Father and the Son. It repeats the argument of verse 23 in nearly the same words.

Jesus promises the Spirit of truth who will be with His disciples forever. It is the source of the anointing of verse 20, and shows that what John describes was promised by Christ Himself before He left.

The Holy Spirit will teach all things and remind the disciples of all Jesus said. It explains verse 27: the teaching of the anointing is the Spirit bringing the words of Christ to mind, not a private source of new information.

Many disciples turn back, and Peter answers that the Twelve have nowhere else to go. It is a scene of those who went out and those who remained, and it shows how Jesus Himself handled the departures that John describes.

The vine and the branches give the fullest picture of what it means to remain in Christ and what it means not to. It supports John's use of the verb in verses 24 and 27 and explains the weight placed on endurance.

The promise that all will know the LORD, from the least to the greatest, stands behind verse 27. The new covenant gives every member of God's people a direct knowledge of Him, which is why John can say they have no need of anyone to teach them in the way the deceivers suggest.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is also the story of a long conflict between the truth God speaks and the lie that rivals it. It begins in the garden, where a voice asks 'Did God really say?', and the lie there is a denial of what God has said and of what God is like. John's 'liar' and 'antichrist' stand in that line. Jesus says in John 8:44 that the devil is the father of lies, and 1 John 2:22 puts the climactic lie in one sentence: that Jesus is not the Christ.

The Old Testament shows the same pattern in the form of false prophets who rise within Israel, and in the pagan kings who exalt themselves above every god. Each time the question is whether God's people will hold to what God has spoken. The story reaches its turning point in the coming of Jesus, who is the Truth, John 14:6, and who is anointed with the Spirit for a ministry that He then shares with His people. After His ascension the conflict continues, now in the setting of the church. John's 'last hour' is the age that began with the first coming of Christ and ends with the second, and in it the lie takes many human faces while the Spirit keeps teaching.

The passage sets up what follows in several ways. It leads straight into the discussion of what it means to be children of God, 2:28 to 3:10, where remaining in Christ is again the condition of confidence at His appearing. It also prepares for the test of the spirits in chapter 4. Beyond the letter, it looks toward Revelation, where the conflict between the Lamb and the beast is drawn on a larger canvas, and where the faithful are those who hold to the testimony of Jesus.

In the new creation the lie will have no place. The one who 'will be revealed' will be destroyed by the Lord Jesus, 2 Thessalonians 2:8, and nothing false will enter the city. What John promises in verse 25, eternal life, will then be fully possessed. The believers who stayed with what they heard from the beginning will find that the promise they held on to was the end of the story as well. The anointing that teaches now will give way to seeing Him face to face, Revelation 22:4, and the truth that was heard will be the truth that is seen.

sermon.title: A Word of Warning
sermon.why: Begg preaches this passage, 1 John 2:18-27, on the last hour, the antichrists who deny the Son, and the anointing that keeps believers in the truth. A clear, orthodox handling of discernment and assurance.

quiz.q: How does John explain the false teachers leaving the church?

options.text: They went out because they never truly belonged to us.
options.note: Verse 19: their departure showed they were never really of the fellowship.

options.text: They left because the church treated them unfairly.
options.note: John locates the cause in their not belonging, not in mistreatment.

options.text: They were true believers who simply lost interest.
options.note: John says plainly they did not belong to us; their leaving revealed it.

options.text: They moved on to plant other faithful churches.
options.note: They were deceivers, not faithful workers; their departure exposed them.

quiz.q: According to John, who is the liar and the antichrist?

options.text: The one who denies that Jesus is the Christ, thereby denying the Father and the Son.
options.note: Verse 22 defines the antichrist by denial of Jesus as the Christ.

options.text: Anyone who disagrees about minor matters of practice.
options.note: The issue is the central confession of Christ, not minor differences.

options.text: Only a single future world ruler yet to appear.
options.note: John does mention a coming antichrist, but here he stresses the many present deniers of the Son.

options.text: Anyone outside the church who has never believed.
options.note: John speaks of deceivers who denied Christ, not of unbelievers in general.

quiz.q: What does John say about the relationship between the Son and the Father in verse 23?

options.text: Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son has the Father too.
options.note: The Father cannot be had apart from the Son.

options.text: You can have the Father without the Son if you are sincere.
options.note: John says the opposite; denying the Son forfeits the Father.

options.text: The Son matters less than the Father.
options.note: John binds them together; to have one is to have the other.

options.text: The Father and Son are the same person with no distinction.
options.note: John distinguishes Father and Son while binding them together; this blurs that distinction.

quiz.q: What does John mean that believers 'do not need anyone to teach you' (verse 27)?

options.text: They do not need the deceivers' new teaching, for the Spirit confirms the truth they already have.
options.note: The point guards against false teachers, not against all faithful teaching, which John himself gives.

options.text: Believers need no human teachers of any kind, only the Spirit.
options.note: The Spirit does teach believers directly, but the verse does not rule out all human teachers, as John's own teaching shows.

options.text: The Spirit's anointing removes any need to test teaching.
options.note: John urges testing the spirits in 4:1; the anointing does not cancel discernment.

options.text: Believers should reject Scripture and follow feelings.
options.note: John points them to the truth heard from the beginning, not to feelings against Scripture.

quiz.q: What is the promise John highlights for those who remain in the truth?

options.text: Eternal life, the promise Christ Himself made.
options.note: Verse 25 names eternal life as the promise for those who remain in the Son.

options.text: A trouble-free life in this world.
options.note: John promises eternal life, not freedom from trouble now.

options.text: Special status above other believers.
options.note: The promise is eternal life for all who confess the Son, not elite status.

options.text: Complete understanding of every mystery now.
options.note: The Spirit teaches them the truth, but the promise named is eternal life, not exhaustive knowledge now.

questions: John says the departure of the false teachers showed they never truly belonged. How does this help you think about people who once professed faith and then walked away from Christ?
The antichrist is defined by denying that Jesus is the Christ. Where do you encounter subtle denials of who Jesus is today, and how do you recognise them?
Believers have an anointing that teaches them the truth. How have you experienced the Spirit confirming the truth about Jesus and steadying you against error?
John urges that what you heard from the beginning must remain in you. What practices help the core truths of the gospel stay lodged in your heart over the long haul?
To have the Son is to have the Father. How does the promise of eternal life for those who hold to Christ shape the way you face doubt, pressure, or deception?

translationNotes.note: 'The last hour' is the whole era between Christ's first and second comings, not a prediction of an immediate end; the many antichrists are a sign that this final age has arrived.

'All of you know the truth' follows a manuscript reading; the BSB footnote notes a variant, 'you know all things', in some texts. The assurance that believers are taught by the anointing is unchanged.
'You do not need anyone to teach you' is set against the deceivers offering new teaching; it does not forbid faithful instruction, which John is himself giving throughout the letter.
